{"id": "56:78/q02", "question": "What is the hidden book?", "turns_on": "Whether the book is a heavenly archetype, a human manuscript, earlier scripture, an inward locus, or a metaphor for the divine source; some reports allow more than one locus.", "positions": [{"id": "56:78/q02/p1", "position": "It is the heavenly book, specifically the Preserved Tablet.", "reasons": "Muqātil places it at God's right hand beside the Throne, hidden from creatures. Al-Ṭabarī, Mujāhid, Jābir ibn Zayd, Abū Nuhayk, Ibn ʿAbbās, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, and Salmān give its heavenly location; Salmān says only angels touch it. Al-Zajjāj and the many named exegetes identify the Tablet; al-Thaʿlabī and al-Baghawī say it is guarded from devils. Al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī cite 85:21–22; al-Rāzī answers the objection that a tablet cannot be called a book by comparing names of receptacles. Kashshāf, al-Nasafī, al-Bursawī and al-Ālūsī restrict access to purified or near angels. Study Quran reports that it contains every revealed book; Kuran Yolu calls this a spiritual description of the Qur'an's exalted status, and al-Sāmarrāʾī invokes the angelic referent. Al-Ālūsī particularly favors this identification."}, {"id": "56:78/q02/p2", "position": "It is the written Qur'an in people's hands, the Muslim codices.", "reasons": "Mujāhid and Qatāda are reported for this view. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān say that, because codices did not yet exist, this would report the unseen; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says their protection lasts to Resurrection and touching may mean touching manuscripts or figuratively the angels. Al-Ālūsī likewise calls it foreknowledge and says the codices are guarded from alteration. Al-Biqāʿī includes purified, honored codices among several loci. Kashshāf derives a rule about handling the written copy from this reading."}, {"id": "56:78/q02/p3", "position": "It is the Torah and Gospel, or the earlier revealed scriptures as a class.", "reasons": "ʿIkrima says the Torah and Gospel mention the Qur'an and its messenger; Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān say this makes the Qur'an's honor attested by earlier revelation, with Ibn ʿAṭiyya citing 9:36. Al-Rāzī includes other earlier scriptures. Al-Ālūsī reports ʿIkrima through ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Jarīr, and says 'book' must then be generic; his quotation of al-Baḥr makes the Qur'an's honor and nobility the content mentioned there."}, {"id": "56:78/q02/p4", "position": "It is the Psalms.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī reports this as another view; al-Qurṭubī attributes it to al-Suddī."}, {"id": "56:78/q02/p5", "position": "It is the Prophet's heart, where Qur'anic intellect is lodged beyond the senses.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī describes the Qur'an as exalted, ancient, honorable comprehensive knowledge; only purified angels reach what is deposited in the Prophet's heart. He quotes Jesus that knowledge is placed in hearts and manifests through spiritual manners before God, rather than coming down from heaven, rising from earth, or crossing seas."}, {"id": "56:78/q02/p6", "position": "It is the first Spirit, locus of decree and abode of the Muhammadan Spirit.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī offers this as one inward alternative."}, {"id": "56:78/q02/p7", "position": "It is the Muhammadan Spirit itself.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī offers this as the other inward alternative."}, {"id": "56:78/q02/p8", "position": "It is the heart of the believer.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this anonymous suggestion and dismisses it."}, {"id": "56:78/q02/p9", "position": "It figuratively names the Qur'an's correspondence with God's concealed knowledge, will, and command.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the wording and meanings correspond to what God knew and willed and to the command conveyed to the angel. He also calls 'book' a metaphor for fixed, unalterable reality, and cites a poetic fragment for this use."}, {"id": "56:78/q02/p10", "position": "It resides together in the Preserved Tablet, honored hearts, and purified codices.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī describes these as concurrent locations of the precious, fixed, protected Qur'an, safe from alteration."}]}
{"id": "56:78/q03", "question": "What does maknūn say about the book?", "turns_on": "Whether the guarding is against damage or falsehood, concealment from sight, concealment of meanings, figurative exaltation, or protection specifically from alteration.", "positions": [{"id": "56:78/q03/p1", "position": "It is guarded or preserved from harm, falsehood, alteration, and corrupting access.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī and Mujāhid specify dust and earthly contact; al-Thaʿlabī mentions devils and stains. Al-Māwardī reports Mujāhid's 'preserved' and Yaʿqūb from Mujāhid's protection from falsehood; al-Qurṭubī gives both protection with God and protection against falsehood. Al-Rāzī calls the protection complete, explaining that precious things are hidden, and distinguishes the written Qur'an's protection from alteration and corrupting hands. Al-Biqāʿī places it in the Tablet, hearts and codices; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites 85:21–22 against alteration or replacement. Al-Ālūsī reports a narrower alteration-only reading citing 15:9, but favors earlier explanations."}, {"id": "56:78/q03/p2", "position": "It is hidden from creatures' sight and access, apart from selected or purified angels.", "reasons": "Muqātil says hidden from creation; Ibn al-Jawzī transmits him. Al-Rāzī says the Tablet is literally concealed except to chosen angels and uses 56:79 against the ancient-lore charge. Kashshāf, al-Nasafī, al-Bursawī and al-Ālūsī mention near or purified angels. Al-Qāshānī locates the inward knowledge beyond the senses. Study Quran reports that concealment excludes any influence except God's."}, {"id": "56:78/q03/p3", "position": "Its meanings are concealed within it.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī reports this further possibility."}, {"id": "56:78/q03/p4", "position": "Concealment figuratively expresses its lofty rank.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says this is possible if the Torah and Gospel are meant, because what is exalted is concealed."}, {"id": "56:78/q03/p5", "position": "It means only that the book is protected from alteration.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this explanation with 15:9 but prefers the earlier explanations, especially the Preserved Tablet."}]}
{"id": "56:78/q04", "question": "How does 'in a hidden book' relate to the preceding description of the Qur'an?", "turns_on": "The attachment of the prepositional phrase and whether 'in' expresses literal location or figurative correspondence.", "positions": [{"id": "56:78/q04/p1", "position": "The Qur'an itself is described as being in a book.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī identifies that book as the Preserved Tablet and prefers this reading as most strongly honoring the heavenly recited text, while allowing all readings. Al-Ālūsī calls the adjectival construal more eloquent."}, {"id": "56:78/q04/p2", "position": "The phrase qualifies 'noble': the Qur'an is noble in the book even if disbelievers deny its nobility.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī and al-Ālūsī give this syntactic reading; al-Ālūsī favors the adjectival construal instead."}, {"id": "56:78/q04/p3", "position": "The whole description 'noble Qur'an' is the content written in the book.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī compares the statement about ʿIlliyyūn in 83:19."}, {"id": "56:78/q04/p4", "position": "The locative 'in' figuratively expresses correspondence with the divine original.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the containment honorific metaphor: the heard Qur'an's wording and meanings match God's knowledge, will, power and divinely made eloquent discourse. He prefers this to rational-metonymic attribution of the counterpart and cites 6:59, 35:11, and 87:18–19."}, {"id": "56:78/q04/p5", "position": "The Qur'an's description is rational-metonymically attributed to its counterpart.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr mentions this analysis only to prefer the figurative locative instead."}]}
{"id": "56:78/q05", "question": "What status does the hidden book give the Qur'an?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "56:78/q05/p1", "position": "It attests the Qur'an's exalted honor, divine source, and secure preservation.", "reasons": "Kashshāf calls it excellent in kind, beneficial, or honored by God. Ibn Kathīr says both Qur'an and book are exalted, guarded and honored. Al-Biqāʿī says preciousness explains its fixation and protection across Tablet, hearts and codices. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī relates the guarded tablet, exalted wise source and protected book to enduring realities behind the meanings. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the Prophet's recitation matches the miraculous discourse God willed, confirming divine speech rather than human composition. Iṣlāḥī treats 75–96 and the oath as proclaiming exalted revelation shielded from Satan, jinn and devils, accessible to pure near angels; Quraysh risk doom by ignoring it. Kuran Yolu calls the Tablet description spiritual exaltation."}]}
{"id": "56:78/q06", "question": "Which charges against the Qur'an does this wording answer?", "turns_on": "Which reported accusation the book's concealment and protection is invoked to rebut.", "positions": [{"id": "56:78/q06/p1", "position": "It rebuts the charge that jinn or devils supplied the revelation.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says the angel received it from a book before delivering it, so it is not even angelic speech, much less jinn speech. Iṣlāḥī says only pure near angels access the protected book. Study Quran says its concealment excludes influence by anyone but God."}, {"id": "56:78/q06/p2", "position": "It rebuts the charge that the Qur'an is ancient lore taken from open books.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī contrasts those books with the concealed book touched only by the purified, citing 56:79. Study Quran reports the ancient-fables accusations and cites 6:25, 8:31, 16:24, 23:83, 25:5, 27:68, 46:17, 68:15 and 83:13."}]}

ook imply origination, or describe an ancient inward knowledge.", "positions": [{"id": "56:78/q07/p1", "position": "It is originated rather than eternal.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī says the descriptions discourse, revelation, guarded book and untouched fit neither literal nor figurative eternity."}, {"id": "56:78/q07/p2", "position": "It is ancient, honorable comprehensive knowledge.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī describes that knowledge as lodged in the Prophet's heart beyond sense perception, except to purified angels."}]}
{"id": "56:78/q08", "question": "What rule about touching the Qur'an is drawn if the book is the written copy?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "56:78/q08/p1", "position": "Only someone ritually pure should touch the written Qur'an; some extend this to recitation.", "reasons": "Kashshāf draws the rule conditionally from taking the protected book as the written Qur'an. Ibn ʿAṭiyya notes that touch can refer to manuscripts or figuratively to angels. In Salmān's report the heavenly book is touched only by angels, after which he recited to his visitors whatever Qur'an they requested."}]}
{"id": "56:78/q09", "question": "What claims about abrogation accompany citations of this guarded book?", "turns_on": "The direct disagreement concerns whether naskh can mean copying; the other reported principles give the surrounding abrogation discussion.", "positions": [{"id": "56:78/q09/p1", "position": "The preserved record of revelation supports naskh in the sense of copying or transcription.", "reasons": "Ibn Barakāt al-Saʿdī and al-Saʿīdī support al-Naḥḥās with records of deeds, the Mother Book, and this guarded book; their cited verses include 43:4, 45:29 and 56:78. Al-Suyūṭī also lists transcription among the lexical senses of naskh. Makkī rejects this Qur'anic sense because an abrogating passage uses different words."}, {"id": "56:78/q09/p2", "position": "Naskh may mean transfer, as with inheritance moving to another person.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashī gives inheritance; al-Suyūṭī additionally lists removal, replacement, transformation and transcription, citing 22:52 and 16:101."}, {"id": "56:78/q09/p3", "position": "Copying is not a Qur'anic sense of naskh.", "reasons": "Makkī argues that an abrogating passage does not copy the abrogated wording but has different wording."}, {"id": "56:78/q09/p4", "position": "An interpreter must know abrogating and abrogated passages.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashī and al-Suyūṭī relay the imams' requirement. Their reports of ʿAlī vary between a preacher and a judge: when he lacked knowledge of abrogation, ʿAlī said he was doomed and would doom others."}, {"id": "56:78/q09/p5", "position": "Many scholars wrote dedicated works on abrogation.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashī names Qatāda, Abū ʿUbayd, Abū Dāwūd, al-Naḥḥās and Ibn al-Jawzī among others; al-Suyūṭī also names Ibn al-Anbārī, Makkī and Ibn al-ʿArabī."}, {"id": "56:78/q09/p6", "position": "Abrogation is a facilitative dispensation for this community, specifying a ruling's duration.", "reasons": "Al-Suyūṭī says Muslims accept it; he rejects the Jewish equation with changed divine knowledge and compares changing conditions of life, health and wealth, citing 2:106."}, {"id": "56:78/q09/p7", "position": "Only the Qur'an can abrogate the Qur'an.", "reasons": "Some scholars cite 2:106's better or equal replacement and argue that only the Qur'an can match or surpass it."}]}
{"id": "64:6/q01", "question": "What does dhālika refer to?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "64:6/q01/p1", "position": "The worldly calamity already mentioned, often including the afterlife punishment.", "reasons": "Baydawi, Biqa'i and Ibn Ashur identify the preceding calamity; Nasafi, Bursevi, Alusi and Tabataba'i explicitly include both punishments. Tabataba'i says this independent sentence answers an implied question about their cause."}]}
{"id": "64:6/q02", "question": "Why recall the earlier peoples here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "64:6/q02/p1", "position": "Their fate warns present rejecters that the same rejection may bring the same punishment.", "reasons": "Tabari addresses Quraysh by recalling Noah, Ad, Thamud, Abraham and Lot; Elmalili adds Pharaoh. Ibn Atiyya compares Quraysh's refusal of prophethood and resurrection and envy of the chosen messenger. Ibn Ashur calls the warning an indirect allusion. Biqa'i says the passage identifies the cause of destruction. Study Quran cites 25:7 for the same objection to Muhammad. Bursevi says worldly pain did not expiate these unbelievers though sound reports say believers' misfortunes expiate sins."}]}
{"id": "64:6/q03", "question": "What is the hāʾ in bi-annahu?", "turns_on": "Whether the pronoun has an antecedent or introduces the affair.", "positions": [{"id": "64:6/q03/p1", "position": "A pronoun of the matter, explained by the clause about the messengers and their hearers.", "reasons": "Nahhas calls the clause the predicate of anna; Tabrisī, Samin and Ibn Ashur call the pronoun one of affair. Ibn Ashur says it magnifies the explanation. Biqa'i says the compact form suits a sura concerned with the Hour."}, {"id": "64:6/q03/p2", "position": "A pronoun referring to firmness.", "reasons": "Jishumi records this alternative."}]}
{"id": "64:6/q04", "question": "Why were these peoples punished?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "64:6/q04/p1", "position": "Messengers brought clear proof, but their peoples rejected human guidance and disbelieved.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Tabari, Wahidi, Jishumi, Ibn al-Jawzi, Bursevi, Elmalili and Islahi trace this causal sequence. Qurtubi singles out disbelief of the messengers. Ibn Ashur says rejecting the Messenger and miraculous Quran adds another form of unbelief. Tabataba'i says successive rejected missions left nations as tales, citing 23:44."}]}
{"id": "64:6/q05", "question": "How often did their messengers come, and to whom?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "64:6/q05/p1", "position": "God's chosen messengers came repeatedly to their own peoples with messages intended for them.", "reasons": "Tabataba'i says kana with the imperfect depicts repeated arrivals against one decisive refusal; Asad also says time and again. Biqa'i says God chose each people's messengers and sent them habitually with clear proofs."}]}
{"id": "64:6/q06", "question": "What were al-bayyināt?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "64:6/q06/p1", "position": "Clear explanations and proofs, including arguments, miracles and scriptures, establishing the messengers' truth.", "reasons": "Muqatil calls them explanations; Tabari, Nahhas, Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir call them proofs; Jishumi and Nasafi specify miracles; Biqa'i includes scriptures. Ibn Ashur treats the Quran as a miraculous proof. Islahi calls the arguments sound."}]}
{"id": "64:6/q07", "question": "How does the bāʾ in bil-bayyināt work?", "turns_on": "Accompaniment versus transitivity.", "positions": [{"id": "64:6/q07/p1", "position": "It marks accompaniment: they came with proofs.", "reasons": "Bursevi records the possibility."}, {"id": "64:6/q07/p2", "position": "It makes the verb transitive to the proofs brought.", "reasons": "Bursevi records this other possibility."}]}
{"id": "64:6/q08", "question": "How is fa-qālū joined?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "64:6/q08/p1", "position": "It is coordinated with kānat.", "reasons": "Bursevi states this analysis."}]}
{"id": "64:6/q09", "question": "What does bashar denote here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "64:6/q09/p1", "position": "Human beings as a kind; the word can denote one human or a group.", "reasons": "Mawardi equates bashar with insan, derives bashar from visible skin, and gives insan alternative derivations from sociability or forgetfulness. Baydawi and Ibn Ashur say it can apply to one or many; Ibn Ashur cites 18:110, 12:31, 19:17. Qurtubi cites 12:31. Nahhas reports al-Mazini's contrast with nafar and raht and Muhammad ibn Yazid's objection that bashar itself is singular or plural. Tabataba'i says it is plural here by the following verb."}]}
{"id": "64:6/q10", "question": "What did the objection to human guides express?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "64:6/q10/p1", "position": "They scornfully denied that humans like themselves could be divinely appointed guides.", "reasons": "Tabari and Mawardi stress contempt; Wahidi, Ibn Kathir and Qurtubi stress incredulity. Nasafi and Razi note that they accepted stone worship while denying human messengers. Abu Hayyan says they assumed all humans equal. Biqa'i says envy and misplaced pride led them to think divine greatness required angels, though ordinary humans could not bear seeing angels and receive humans better. Jishumi calls the objection evasive in face of miracle. Ibn Ashur cites 25:7 and 17:95 for human capacity and divine choice. Tabataba'i reads indefinite bashar as belittling. Asad associates distrust with moral estrangement. Study Quran lists parallels including 17:94 and 54:24; Kuranyolu cites 14:10-11, 18:110, 23:24, 23:33 and 25:7; Bursevi and Alusi compare Thamud's 54:24."}]}
{"id": "64:6/q11", "question": "How is abashar parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether the question is a nominal clause or has an implied verb.", "positions": [{"id": "64:6/q11/p1", "position": "Nominative bashar is the subject, with yahdūnanā its predicate.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya and Tabrisī allow an indefinite subject in a nonassertive question; Abu Hayyan and Alusi report al-Hawfi and Ibn Atiyya's analysis. Qurtubi and Samin also give it. Ibn Ashur says fronting intensifies denial."}, {"id": "64:6/q11/p2", "position": "Nominative bashar is the agent of an omitted verb explained by yahdūnanā, through ishtighāl.", "reasons": "Tabrisī, Abu Hayyan, Samin, Biqa'i, Bursevi and Alusi cite the interrogative hamza's preference for a verb. Burhan contrasts accusative abasharan in 54:24, where the resumed object is accusative, with nominative here, where it is subject."}]}

{"id": "64:6/q14", "question": "What guidance did they reject?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "64:6/q14/p1", "position": "Guidance in religion toward God or nearness to Him.", "reasons": "Bursevi gives these possible scopes; Asad notes the literal reply guide us."}]}
{"id": "64:6/q15", "question": "What did disbelief and turning away entail?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "64:6/q15/p1", "position": "They denied messengers and truth and refused faith, proofs, reflection, admonition or action.", "reasons": "Nahhas names prophets and signs; Mawardi the messengers and proof; Tabrisī, Baydawi and Alusi reflecting on signs; Ibn Kathir acting on truth. {"id": "64:6/q16", "question": "What does fa-kafarū wa-tawallaw emphasize?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "64:6/q16/p1", "position": "Their disbelief followed immediately without reflection, and turning away adds complete refusal.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and Biqa'i read the fa as immediate; Razi says the second verb is not redundant but describes total rejection."}]}
{"id": "64:6/q17", "question": "What does wa-staghnā Allāh mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the clause names timeless independence or how it becomes manifest.", "positions": [{"id": "64:6/q17/p1", "position": "God had no need of their faith, worship, obedience, deeds, charity or any creature.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Tabari, Wahidi, Razi and others stress timeless independence. Mawardi and Qurtubi report Muqatil grounding it in sovereignty; Mawardi reports al-Bara's mention of charity. Jishumi, Tabrisī, Biqa'i and Islahi say commands and messengers benefit people. Qashani grounds it in divine essence. Tabataba'i reports but rejects this as the specific explanation here."}, {"id": "64:6/q17/p2", "position": "God displayed His existing independence by destroying them and ending their line.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan say destruction made it manifest. Bursevi and Alusi argue He would not have destroyed them if He needed their obedience. Elmalili agrees. Tabataba'i's narrower explanation says destruction refutes their confidence in knowledge, strength and survival, citing 18:35 and 41:50."}, {"id": "64:6/q17/p3", "position": "He did not compel belief although He had power to do so.", "reasons": "Razi quotes Kashshaf; Abu Hayyan calls Zamakhshari's analysis a Mu'tazili insinuation. Kuranyolu transmits Zamakhshari and Shawkani; Study Quran reports R and Z."}, {"id": "64:6/q17/p4", "position": "Clear proof made any renewed summons unnecessary.", "reasons": "Mawardi, Tabrisī and Qurtubi give this alternative; Ibn Ashur says proof was enough absent obstinacy and punishment was hastened. Tabataba'i reports then rejects it."}, {"id": "64:6/q17/p5", "position": "Worldly and final consequences show God owes people no happiness or favor.", "reasons": "Tabataba'i prefers this broader explanation to the destruction-only one, citing 41:50 and 18:36; both show majesty and power."}]}
{"id": "64:6/q18", "question": "What does the form istaghnā contribute?", "turns_on": "How the added letters relate to God's eternal sufficiency.", "positions": [{"id": "64:6/q18/p1", "position": "Form X intensifies or manifests already complete sufficiency, without seeking or acquiring it.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya notes Form X commonly seeks, but says manifestation fits; Abu Hayyan denies seeking, Samin quotes Zamakhshari that sin is no request marker, Ibn Ashur says sin and ta intensify and cites 39:7, and Tabataba'i says God cannot acquire wealth."}, {"id": "64:6/q18/p2", "position": "It can be understood from the triliteral as full independence because seeking entails need.", "reasons": "Bursevi reports Sa'di al-Mufti's analysis."}]}
{"id": "64:6/q19", "question": "How is wa-staghnā connected syntactically?", "turns_on": "Coordination versus circumstance.", "positions": [{"id": "64:6/q19/p1", "position": "The waw coordinates this with the preceding sequence.", "reasons": "Alusi prefers coordination."}, {"id": "64:6/q19/p2", "position": "The waw introduces a circumstantial clause about God's preexisting independence.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur cites eternity; Bursevi reports Sa'di al-Mufti's understood qad. Alusi reports the alternative but prefers coordination."}]}
{"id": "64:6/q20", "question": "What does ghanī affirm?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "64:6/q20/p1", "position": "God is intrinsically independent of all creation and everything requested of them.", "reasons": "Tabari, Baydawi, Nasafi, Biqa'i and others generalize independence. Elmalili says God could replace the universe; Qashani says His perfection needs no human knowledge; Tabataba'i calls intrinsic richness the ground of the judgment."}]}
{"id": "64:6/q21", "question": "What does hamīd affirm?", "turns_on": "Intrinsic worthiness, actual praise received, or God's relation to praise.", "positions": [{"id": "64:6/q21/p1", "position": "He is intrinsically worthy of praise for perfection, blessings and just or beneficent acts, even if no one praises Him.", "reasons": "Mawardi gives this alternative to actual praise; Jishumi, Razi, Tabrisī, Baydawi, Biqa'i, Elmalili and Tabataba'i stress deserved praise. Bursevi defines praise as naming perfect attributes and links it to remembrance. Study Quran cites the pairing with Self-Sufficiency at 4:131, 14:8, 22:64, 31:12, 31:26, 35:15 and 60:6. {"id": "66:6/q01", "question": "What should a reader make of the address to believers?", "turns_on": "Whether faith here identifies sincere believers or includes merely verbal profession.", "positions": [{"id": "66:6/q01/p1", "position": "It calls believers to heed a command or prohibition and reform themselves and their households.", "reasons": "Ibn Masʿūd expects a command or prohibition after this address; al-Burhān urges pause, reflection, acceptance, and repentance. {"id": "66:6/q02", "question": "What does قُوا۟ mean?", "turns_on": "Whether 'protecting' names direct safeguarding or admonition figuratively.", "positions": [{"id": "66:6/q02/p1", "position": "Guard or preserve yourselves from harm and the Fire.", "reasons": "Jishumī defines wiqāya as guarding and preserving; al-Māwardī adduces a rajaz line for protection; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says to interpose a safeguard; Ṭabāṭabāʾī defines protection against injury; Bursevī calls it keeping safe and distant."}, {"id": "66:6/q02/p2", "position": "The command can be understood as admonition and warning that save from punishment.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr treats admonition either as the cause of protection or as a forceful metaphor equating the two."}]}
{"id": "66:6/q03", "question": "How is the form قُوا۟ derived?", "turns_on": "The proposed phonological environment versus a transitivity rule, and counterexamples.", "positions": [{"id": "66:6/q03/p1", "position": "It comes from وقى يقي; the initial wāw drops between yāʾ and kasra.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās gives the underlying وقى يوقي. {"id": "66:6/q08", "question": "What does protection of the family require?", "turns_on": "Whether the imperative emphasizes a householder's instruction or each family member's own protective act.", "positions": [{"id": "66:6/q08/p1", "position": "Teach, advise, discipline, command obedience and right, forbid sin, and help family members practice duties.", "reasons": "ʿAlī emphasizes teaching and discipline, Qatāda supervision and restraint, Mujāhid fear of God, Ibn ʿAbbās remembrance and prayer. ʿUmar's question elicits the Prophet's command to enjoin what God commands and forbid what He forbids. {"id": "66:6/q25", "question": "What do غِلَاظٌ and شِدَادٌ mean of the angels?", "turns_on": "Whether the adjectives describe bodily constitution, harsh conduct, or nearly synonymous severity.", "positions": [{"id": "66:6/q25/p1", "position": "Harsh in heart, speech or treatment, and strong in body or action.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās and al-Baghawī emphasize harshness toward sinners; Ibn ʿAṭiyya compares 3:159. Al-Qurṭubī reports harsh speech and forceful action, severe seizure, or immense bodies. Al-Bayḍāwī gives harsh speech/strong action or nature/power. Abū Ḥayyān gives massive bodies or harsh conduct. Ibn ʿĀshūr derives the plurals from غليظ and شديد, describing roughness metaphorically and strength in harmful action. Ibn Kathīr says mercy was removed from their hearts and appearance is frightening. Bursevī says pleas cannot soften them. Al-Qāshānī reads their merciless strength as their innate constitution for overpowering, from which they take pleasure."}, {"id": "66:6/q25/p2", "position": "They describe the angels' moral qualities and conduct rather than their spiritual substance.", "reasons": "Rāzī prefers this because angels are spirits; he allows severity toward God's enemies with mercy toward allies, citing 48:29. {"id": "66:6/q26", "question": "What reports describe the keepers' size, number, and force?", "turns_on": "The reports give different spans, numbers and force.", "positions": [{"id": "66:6/q26/p1", "position": "A keeper's shoulders span a year's journey; a blow or shove drives seventy thousand into Hell.", "reasons": "Muqātil adds a mace blow scatters bones and a forty-year fall; Ibn ʿAbbās is cited by al-Wāḥidī, Ibn al-Jawzī and al-Qurṭubī. Al-Baghawī and Biqāʿī give a shove or throw of seventy thousand."}, {"id": "66:6/q26/p2", "position": "A keeper's shoulders span east to west.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī transmits a Prophetic report through Ibn Wahb and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd."}, {"id": "66:6/q26/p3", "position": "Nineteen keepers each have a two-hundred-year shoulder span.", "reasons": "Abū ʿImrān al-Jawnī says they lack mercy, were created for punishment and crush with one blow."}, {"id": "66:6/q26/p4", "position": "Hell's first gate has four hundred thousand dark-faced keepers, followed by nineteen larger keepers and similar hosts at later gates.", "reasons": "ʿIkrima says gates are five hundred years of descent apart."}]}
{"id": "66:6/q27", "question": "Why describe the angels as harsh and powerful?", "turns_on": "The threat's force and the rhetoric of masculine agreement.", "positions": [{"id": "66:6/q27/p1", "position": "Their harshness makes punishment inexorable and follows God's order.", "reasons": "Muqātil says this counters Abū al-Ashdayn's boast of defeating seventeen guardians. Ibn ʿĀshūr says obedience after harshness balances aversion and shows the severity is commanded; Biqāʿī says it is measured to guilt."}, {"id": "66:6/q27/p2", "position": "Strength and severity shape masculine grammatical agreement in descriptions of angels.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī says masculine forms suit the harsher of two punishments, comparing 8:50, 47:27, 25:25, 41:30 and 97:4."}]}
{"id": "66:6/q28", "question": "What does لَّا يَعْصُونَ ٱللَّهَ say of the angels?", "turns_on": "Personal obedience to commands versus an inward account of cosmological necessity.", "positions": [{"id": "66:6/q28/p1", "position": "They never refuse, exceed, diminish, or otherwise violate God's commands.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī and al-Qurṭubī specify no addition or omission; Ibn al-Jawzī reports not exceeding; Biqāʿī says always and contrasts fallible humans who forget times, pillars or conditions. Biqāʿī quotes a Prophetic exhortation, transmitted by Ibn Mājah and al-Ṭayālisī without grading, that humans should be upright even though they cannot attain perfection."}, {"id": "66:6/q28/p2", "position": "Their obedience is innate submission of lower powers to the Divine Presence.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says the powers overpower bodies while being overpowered by God; this enables their effects in the world."}]}
{"id": "66:6/q29", "question": "What does وَيَفْعَلُونَ مَا يُؤْمَرُونَ add?", "turns_on": "Timing and completeness of the action, with grammatical reinforcement.", "positions": [{"id": "66:6/q29/p1", "position": "They carry out each command promptly, completely, at its appointed time, without delay or reluctance.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī and al-Qurṭubī specify neither early nor late; Ibn Kathīr adds complete ability and no moment's delay; Bursevī says without omission or addition. {"id": "66:6/q30", "question": "How do the two clauses about angelic obedience relate?", "turns_on": "Whether the difference is inward/outward, rhetorical emphasis, time, or object of duty.", "positions": [{"id": "66:6/q30/p1", "position": "The first concerns inward acceptance without refusal; the second outward, prompt performance.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf's distinction is repeated by Rāzī, al-Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn, and Ālūsī.
